walkthroughs.body_html:
Food Science — a core area of GCSE Food Preparation and Nutrition.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Food Science brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Food Science.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

The food is organic.

Calories, Carbs, Calcium, Cholesterol.

mcqs.q: On a traffic-light label, what does a red light indicate?
options: The food is organic.
High amounts of that nutrient per 100g - eat less often.
Carbohydrate.
The food is dangerous and should never be eaten.

mcqs.q: Which vitamin is most likely to be deficient in a poorly planned vegan diet?

Vitamin C.

mcqs.q: The deep brown, savoury crust that forms when a steak is seared in a hot dry pan is caused by:
options: Gelatinisation of starch
The Maillard reaction between proteins and sugars
Emulsification of the fat
Fermentation by yeast

mcqs.q: When egg whites are whisked into a stiff foam for meringue, the whisking:
options: Denatures the proteins, which unfold and trap air bubbles
Gelatinises the proteins
Converts the protein into sugar
Caramelises the egg white

mcqs.q: A custard made with cornflour thickens as it is heated because:
options: The starch granules absorb liquid, swell and burst - gelatinisation
The milk proteins evaporate
Air is whisked into the mixture
The cornflour melts into the milk

mcqs.q: A student uses bicarbonate of soda alone (with no acid) in a plain scone mixture. What is the likely result?
options: The scones will not rise at all
A soapy, bitter taste and yellowish colour
The scones will be extra light with no flavour change
The mixture will turn to liquid
